content: Has anyone tried implementing Conway's Game of Life in Lean? Or, for that matter, any cellular automata? I think it would be a very neat project to formalize the Turing Completeness of Game of Life.
How would you formalize that statement? I'm aware that it's possible to simulate arbitrary circuits within CGL but I don't know which precise predicate would be indicative of that fact.

I would assume something along the lines of. Given some turing machine there exists an initial configuration of a GoL that, when some cells of it are initialized with some encoding of the TM input, produces an encoded version of the TM output for all input/output pairs.

You can also prove that the language {⟨board,n⟩∣after n steps, the cell at the origin is alive}\{ ⟨board, n⟩ \mid \text{after }n\text{ steps, the cell at the origin is alive} \}{⟨board,n⟩∣after n steps, the cell at the origin is alive} is RERERE-complete, I think. Or maybe instead of n being in the word the condition needs to be ∃ n, ....

@Snir Broshi Yes, I think the language needs to be {B∣the origin cell is alive at some point during the evolution of  B}\{ B | \text{the origin cell is alive at some point during the evolution of } B \}{B∣the origin cell is alive at some point during the evolution of  B}. The language you gave is clearly decidable (just evolve the board for n steps) so it is not RE-hard.

Actually proving such a statement reduces the method @Henrik Böving suggests--embedding a Turing machine into Game of Life (which is exactly what Conway did in 1982). Then to prove that the language {B∣∃n,B.origin is alive after n steps}\{ B | ∃ n, B\text{.origin is alive after n steps} \}{B∣∃n,B.origin is alive after n steps} is RE-hard, you can prove that the halting problem is reducible to this language. In Lean, this would probably look like:

-- takes a turing machine and produces a board which encodes that TM
def Turing.FinTM2.toGameOfLife (tm : FinTM2) : GameOfLifeBoard := sorry

-- the turing machine halts iff the origin cell is eventually alive
theorem TM2toGameOfLife_halts (tm : FinTM2) : tm.halts ↔ ∃ n, (tm.toGameOfLife.step n).origin.isAlive := sorry

That doesn't prove the language is RE-hard though, unless you're counting Lean proofs as Turing machines (of course, they technically are, but you can't prove it inside Lean itself). To be RE-complete you have to demonstrate a TM that performs the reduction (using some Primcodable GameOfLifeBoard).
Although I don't know enough about TMs in mathlib to know if that's possible with what we have, I couldn't find Primcodable FinTM2.
For inspiration, there was a neat formalization of GOL in HOL published last year: https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITP.2025.25

Snir Broshi said:

That doesn't prove the language is RE-hard though, unless you're counting Lean proofs as Turing machines (of course, they technically are, but you can't prove it inside Lean itself). To be RE-complete you have to demonstrate a TM that performs the reduction (using some Primcodable GameOfLifeBoard).

Yes, good point, the reduction FinTM2.toGameOfLife needs to be many-to-one. As long as it does not use noncomputable (which it shouldn't, it's just constructing a cellular automata) it should be be easy in principle to show that it can be performed by a TM. But I also don't know about about TMs in Mathlib to say for sure if this is possible.
If you just want a proof that some Lean function is computable, there's my https://github.com/Rob23oba/dependent-computability. I'd be happy to improve on it if the want is there
